FEDERAL POWER COMMISSION WASHINGTON, D.C. 20426
IN REPLY REFER TO:
JUN 18 1971
Mr. Charles J. Crlebeke
Deputy Under Secretary
Department of Housing and
Urban Development
Washington, D. C. 20410
Dear Mr. Orlebele:
This is in reference to your letter of April 9, 1971, requesting comments of the Federal Power Commission on the Draft Environmental Statement, Operation Breakthrough, April 9, 1971.
In accordance with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and the role of expertise assigned to the Federal Power Commission by the Guidelines of the Council on Environmental Quality dated April 23, 1971, our commerts will be focused as you suggest on the general Breakthrough effort and, as such, will take up the technical characteristics of total energy systems and the environmental consequences of use of such systems in large housing projects. Since your referral speaks for the most part ir generalities, these comments should not be misconstrued as being addressed to specific housing projects briefly mentioned or as related to a detailed analysis as required by Section 102 (2) (C) of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969.
With regard to Section 5 of the Draft Statement entitled "Advanced Utility Systems Demonstration", pages 21 and 22, it should be noted that there is a body of literature and accumulated operating experience regarding the validity of these systems as elements of design of large housing projects. The Statement also appears to justify support of total energy systems on the ground that such systems contribute to air quality improvement by reducing fuel consumption for required energy demand.
Total energy systems -- those which are designed to generate electricity and to use exhaust heat or steam for hot water heating and space heating and cooling or for process heat -- have been on the industrial scene for many years. More recently oil and gas fueled total energy systems have been designed using diesel, gas turbine or gas engine prime movers to serve apartment complemes, educational institutions, and suburban shopping centers.
